findings.title: Findings converge on the transition-observer layer (OutageLog's transition feed, the sync observer list, its payload and its replay)
findings.why_it_matters: Six findings from both critics land on one mechanism: the layer this design adds between `set_connection_state` and its consumers. That layer is D1-A (OutageLog's state facts come from transitions, while its per-attempt and per-recheck calls stay explicit), D2's new sync observer list, D3's `ConnectionTransition` payload, and D5's replay on registration. The findings come at it from different angles. OutageLog ends up with two drivers whose order is unwritten (Finding 2). "Connected since" and "ever connected" get a second owner inside OutageLog (Finding 3). The payload isn't checked against what the planned second observer, the #3678 history writer, needs (Finding 4). The replay serves a consumer whose ratified spec doesn't want it (Finding 5). The transition handler and `record_core_wait` both open the episode (Finding 6). And the list is a second observer class beside `ObserverList` (Finding 7). Each finding has its own local fix, and those fixes would add specification, tests and payload fields to a layer whose driver split and consumer fit are still unsettled. The question for you: should the layer be re-evaluated as a whole before any of these are patched? That re-evaluation includes whether OutageLog needs to be a transition observer at all, and whether some of the failure modes are limitations to accept and document.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the transition-observer layer before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions it must answer:
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the transition-observer layer before addressing the converging findings individually

findings.title: OutageLog's episode and gap state is split across two entry points, and the order between them is unwritten
findings.why_it_matters: Today `record_failure` does everything in one method, in a fixed order. It computes the flap before the stable-episode reset, decides `first_in_episode` after the reset, then opens the gap with `gap_after_flap` from the same flap (`websocket_reconnect.py:268-281`). D1-A moves the flap, stable-reset and gap-opening steps into a transition handler that runs when the state leaves CONNECTED, and keeps `record_failure` for the per-attempt work. `record_failure` then reads what the handler left behind, and the result depends on which call ran first. The design doesn't say what the handler writes, what `record_failure` reads, or in which order they run.
findings.recommended: A: Keep OutageLog on its explicit `record_failure`/`record_core_wait`/`record_connected` calls (D1-C), add WAITING_FOR_CORE and the observer list for other consumers, and reword AC3.

findings.title: "Connected since" and "ever connected" get two owners
findings.why_it_matters: D1-A has OutageLog work out `connected_for` from its own `at` and latch "has ever connected" itself, and it removes those arguments from `record_failure`. But `WebsocketService._connected_at` stays for `ReconnectPolicy.on_connection_ended` (Assumed, bullet 4), and `_ever_connected` stays for the first-connect INFO line and `runtime_query_service.py:400`. `record_failure` and `record_core_wait` still need `has_ever_connected` for `maybe_summarize` and `FIRST_CONNECT_HINT` (`websocket_reconnect.py:301, 312, 378`). So OutageLog has to keep a shadow latch and a shadow connected-at timestamp. That is the "parallel model" this change sets out to remove.
findings.recommended: A: Keep `_connected_at` and `_ever_connected` on WebsocketService as the only owners, and give OutageLog `connected_for` and `has_ever_connected` instead of having it infer them.

findings.title: The transition payload isn't checked against what the planned history writer needs
findings.why_it_matters: The design's motivation is the #3678 writer, which the 152 pause note and Gap 2 plan as a second transition observer. The structural-minimalist read spec 152's paused ledger, where D4 and D6 write rows from OutageLog through a callable, and concluded that 152 never becomes a transition observer. That reading is superseded: the pause note says those decisions get revised against #4091. But the architect's underlying point stands. Spec 152's ratified rows (D4 option D, D5 option E) carry:
findings.recommended: B: Before building, lay spec 152's D4/D5 connection rows against the payload. Decide which edge carries the cause on recv death, and whether flap and outage length go on the payload or are derived by the writer. Record the result in D3.

findings.title: D5's replay on registration has no consumer, and its stated beneficiary's spec contradicts it
findings.why_it_matters: D5 replays the current state to each new observer as `ConnectionTransition(old=None, new=<current>, detail=None, at=now)`. That widens `old` to `ConnectionState | None` for every observer. Its only registrant today, OutageLog, registers in `__init__` and ignores the replay (D5 says so). D5's Situation justifies the replay with "#3678's writer ... wants a row with the session's starting connection state". Spec 152's ratified D4 says otherwise: "The last-written state starts empty ... so the first connection writes `connected`". No row at session start. A replay is also indistinguishable from a real event except by `old is None`, and it carries a registration-time monotonic `at`, so a writer has to special-case it.
findings.recommended: A: Drop the replay (D5-A). `old` stays non-optional, and a late-registering consumer reads `connection_state` first.

findings.title: Entering WAITING_FOR_CORE opens the episode in two places
findings.why_it_matters: D1 column A has OutageLog's transition handler "open an episode if none is open" on entering WAITING_FOR_CORE. `record_core_wait`, which D1 keeps on every recheck, already starts with `if self.episode_started_at is None: self.start_episode(now)`. Per D8, the WAITING_FOR_CORE transition sits next to the first `record_core_wait` call in `wait_for_core_running`. So both paths guess whether an episode is open, and the handler's guess is dead code. If one copy is edited alone, the episode opens twice or never, and the summaries stop without any error.

findings.title: The sync observer list is a second class beside `ObserverList`
findings.why_it_matters: D2 adds "a small sync observer list beside `ObserverList`" with the same add, remove and log-and-skip behavior. That copies most of `observer_list.py`'s roughly 25 lines, and a reader has to learn two near-identical contracts. The only part of `ObserverList` that is specific to async is `await observer(*args)`. The minimalist's proposed fix (add a sync `notify` to `ObserverList`) needs the TypeVar bound (`Callable[..., Awaitable[None]]`) widened. That would let a sync callable into a list whose `notify` awaits it, which fails at runtime instead of at type-check time. The systems-architect argued against reopening D2 as its own finding, because D2 was ratified.
findings.recommended: A: Keep the separate small sync class as D2 ratified.

findings.title: The async-announcer follow-up that D2, D7 and D8 lean on has no tracked home
findings.why_it_matters: D2, D7 and D8 each defer the same tidy-up: "a single ordered async announcer consuming transitions". It would absorb the ready reason, the announcement lists, the bus events and the `_observers_announced`/`_bus_announced` flags that each call site now assembles by hand. This change adds to that pile. WAITING_FOR_CORE gets a transition, an explicit `report_connection_status` and a per-recheck `record_core_wait` at one site. Adding any future state means touching the setter, `WS_VALID_TRANSITIONS` and every site's follow-ups. The deferral is ratified, but no open issue tracks it (a search of open issues for "announcer" finds nothing relevant). A follow-up that three decisions cite and nothing tracks is likely to be lost.
findings.recommended: A: File the async-announcer follow-up as an issue, parked with a trigger, and cite its number in D2's ratification.
findings.chosen: A: File the async-announcer follow-up as an issue, parked with a trigger, and cite its number in D2's ratification

findings.title: D9's harness change adds a hidden test-behavior coupling (`_connected_at` unset on harness services)
WAITING_FOR_CORE's exit edges are pinned only as table data, not as behavior
findings.why_it_matters: The CONNECTING and DISCONNECTED exits from WAITING_FOR_CORE exist only in the transition-table test, so a reorder of the failure path or gate fails no test.

findings.title: "No per-attempt state changes" is now false for attempts that reach the core wait
findings.why_it_matters: The WS_VALID_TRANSITIONS comment and the ledger's Assumed bullet claim failed attempts cause no transitions, but an attempt that waits for the core then fails leaves WAITING_FOR_CORE each time.
findings.chosen: Reword the header comment and Assumed bullet; add a #3678 carry-over note in the Build section

findings.title: mark_websocket_service_connected docstring overstates what the setter reports
findings.why_it_matters: Only AUTH_FAILED warns; WAITING_FOR_CORE and CONNECTED starting states are silent, so the docstring promises a warning that won't fire.
findings.chosen: Correct the docstring and D9's Order and scope note to say only AUTH_FAILED warns

findings.title: Connection state and the core-wait reason remain two sources of truth
findings.why_it_matters: The core state being waited on lives only in the ready-reason string; #3678 might parse it.
findings.recommended: A: Keep the ratified split; no change in this PR. #3678 should read the core state from a typed source, not parse the reason text.
findings.chosen: A: Keep the ratified split; no change in this PR. #3678 should read the core state from a typed source, not parse the reason text.

findings.title: The "set state before awaiting report_connection_status" order is not pinned
findings.why_it_matters: A reorder would pass CI; no current consumer reads the state at readiness-wake time.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: The single-writer rule holds by grep at ship time, with nothing enforcing it
findings.why_it_matters: A future direct src/ writer would skip the setter's latch and clears without failing anything.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation
